result.target_topic: Allowance for Credit Losses balance and coverage ratios for consumer and corporate loans
result.target_summary: As of December 31, 2024, the Allowance for Credit Losses (ACLL) was $13.6 billion, representing approximately 22 months of coincident net credit loss coverage based on 4Q24 NCLs, compared to $12.6 billion and 25 months of coverage as of December 31, 2023. Specifically, Branded Cards ACLL as a percentage of EOP loans was 6.4% in 2024 (vs 6.0% in 2023) and Retail Services ACLL as a percentage of EOP loans was 11.3% in 2024 (vs 11.1% in 2023).

materiality_analysis.reason: The disclosure changes from reporting total ACLL amounts and coverage metrics for 2023 and 2024 (in 2024) to reporting total ACLL for 2025 and 2024, and segment-specific percentages for 2025 and 2024. Crucially, the 2024 disclosure included specific 2023 year-end data ($12.6 billion, 25 months coverage), which is largely omitted or de-emphasized in the split 2025 disclosures which focus on the 2025 year-end figures ($13.3 billion, 24 months coverage) and 2024 comparative figures. The removal of the 2023 absolute dollar/coverage context and the shift to segment-specific percentages for the current year represents a meaningful change in the historical comparison data provided to investors.
materiality_analysis.key_change: Shift in historical comparative period data and metric granularity

comparisons.peer_summary: The allowance for credit losses increased by $2.1 billion to $26.9 billion as of December 31, 2024, driven primarily by a $2.2 billion addition in Card Services due to loan growth and vintage seasoning, partially offset by reductions in Home Lending and wholesale.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and JPM report an increase in their Allowance for Credit Losses (ACLL) during 2024, though driven by different primary factors. Citi's ACLL increased to $13.6 billion (22 months coverage), while JPMorgan's ACLL increased to $26.9 billion. JPM explicitly attributes its increase to a $2.2 billion addition in Card Services driven by loan growth and vintage seasoning, whereas Citi's disclosure focuses on the resulting coverage ratios (6.4% for Branded Cards) and total months of coverage without explicitly attributing the dollar change to card loan growth in the same detail.
